bivy.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs

Everything about this approach is currently harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road is closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under an order running to the start of 2028 unless lifted sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. bivy.name: Itswoot Ridge
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.

bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
bivy.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

bivy.name: Upper Diobsud Lakes
bivy.notes: The highest comfortable camp on the massif and the natural pivot for anyone crossing it, in the upper Diobsud Creek basin on the far side of Bacon Peak from the Anderson Creek road. It is the camp a party reaches at the end of a long traverse day, and the one they leave from for the summit, for the ground east toward Berdeen, or for the long line north over the divide toward Hagan and Blum. What sets it apart from every other high site here is that it has water at six thousand feet, which nothing on the connecting ridges does. It is alpine meadow, so the heather is the thing to protect and the tent goes on rock. Snow covers this basin well into July and the lakes can still be part frozen at the start of the season. There is no shelter, no cell coverage, and no quick way down from here in any direction.

bivy.permit: This basin lies on the North Cascades National Park side of the divide, so a park backcountry permit for the correct cross-country zone is required for an overnight, collected in person at the wilderness information center. No campfires. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than in the meadow, keep a hundred feet back from the water, and carry out human waste in a blue bag from snow and glacier ground. The party limit in a park cross-country zone is small — confirm the number when you collect the permit rather than assuming a Forest Service twelve.
bivy.capacity: Room for a small party or two on alpine meadow and heather benches beside the upper pair of lakes; established by use rather than designation, with no facilities

bivy.name: Anderson Creek road end, Watson Lakes trailhead
bivy.notes: This is the road rather than a campsite, because on this side of the massif the road decides what the trip is. It is a rare thing in this range — a driveable gravel road that delivers you to 4,200 ft, within two miles of an alpine lake basin — and it is why the Anderson and Watson Lakes are the substance of this zone rather than a footnote. THE ROAD IS THE PROBLEM AS OF 2026: an atmospheric river in December 2025 cut a washout in FS 1107 at around mile three to four, well below the road end, and that failure has closed the trailhead and the Sno-Park with no quick fix. When it is in force the whole approach becomes four or five miles of road walking with 1,500 ft of gain before the trail even starts, which turns a comfortable overnight on Mount Watson into a serious two-day trip and puts Bacon Peak out of reach for most parties from this side. Confirm the road with the ranger district before driving out, and if it is open, sleeping in the lot the night before is a normal and sensible way to save the morning. The road holds snow late and is not usually driveable to the end until well into the season.
bivy.water: None at the road end. Carry what you need for the evening; the first water is at the lakes, which are close enough that most parties simply walk in.
bivy.permit: Recreation pass required, and a state Sno-Park permit instead from December through April. This is national forest outside the wilderness boundary, so a night in the lot or a pullout is generally tolerated, but never in a way that narrows the road or blocks a turning place. The wilderness rules start at the saddle above.
bivy.capacity: A modest gravel lot at the road end with room for perhaps a dozen vehicles and a few flat spots to sleep beside them; no facilities, and it fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lower Anderson Lake
bivy.notes: Half a mile down from the second trail junction and a hundred feet above the Watson Lakes, and the more useful of the two basins for anyone climbing rather than hiking, because BACON PEAK'S APPROACH RUNS DIRECTLY ABOVE IT. From the saddle about 1.4 miles up the Watson Lakes trail a boot path climbs south onto the ridge high above this lake and opens into the meadows that lead east across the massif toward the Bacon summits, so a party camped here is on the line rather than beside it. It also solves the problem the designated sites create — when the four-and-four at the Watson Lakes are taken there is nowhere legal to squeeze in, and this basin is the fallback. Anderson Butte, a former lookout site with a long view over Baker Lake and across to Baker and Shuksan, is a short spur off the same trail junction and is worth the twenty minutes on an evening you are not going anywhere. Bugs are as bad here as at the lakes over the saddle.
bivy.water: The lake, treated. Dependable all season.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. This lake sits on the trail before it crosses into the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, so the strict designated-site rule that governs the lakes beyond the saddle does not apply in the same way here — but the campfire ban, the small-party expectation and the pack-it-all-out rule should be treated as applying regardless, because the ground is identical and equally fragile. Recreation pass at the trailhead; Sno-Park permit instead from December through April. No permit is issued for an overnight and none is needed.
bivy.capacity: A small number of informal sites at the lake with a backcountry privy; quieter than the sister lakes over the saddle and usually the one with space left

bivy.name: Watson Lakes designated camps
bivy.notes: The substance of this zone and the best camping anywhere near these three peaks. It is a genuinely short walk — about two miles from the road end, through forest to a meadow junction, over a saddle at around 4,700 ft and down to the pair of lakes at 4,400 ft — which makes it the rare alpine camp in the North Cascades that costs a heavy pack almost nothing. Mount Watson rises straight above: from the lakes the line works up the north side, traverses to the large col near 5,900 ft between the East Peak and the jumbled western summits, then takes heather and treed slopes west to the basin under the true summit, a heather and dirt gully on the south side of the summit block, and a short exposed class two to three ridge to the top where many parties want a fixed line. For Bacon Peak this is the staging night rather than the base, since the summit is a long way east across the massif. The lakes are notoriously buggy through midsummer and hold snow into early season. Everything here is heavily used and the designation exists because it was being trampled.
bivy.water: The lakes and a nearby stream, reliable through the season. There is no potable water on the road or the trail, so treat everything.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, inside the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, which the trail enters at the saddle before dropping to the lakes. No overnight permit is required or issued. A recreation pass must be displayed at the trailhead, and between December and April a state Sno-Park permit is required at the Anderson Creek Sno-Park instead. CAMPING IS ALLOWED ONLY IN THE DESIGNATED SITES and campfires are prohibited outright — carry a stove. Standard wilderness rules otherwise: keep the party small, camp on rock or bare ground rather than in the heather, pack out everything, and secure food overnight since there is no hardware provided.
bivy.capacity: Designated sites at the two lakes, first come first served with no reservations, plus a backcountry toilet. Flat ground is mostly rock outcrop along the shoreline; the upper lake takes the larger share of parties.

bivy.name: Northeast Bacon camp, above the glacier
bivy.notes: The high camp for Bacon Peak from the Anderson Creek road, and the reason the peak is a two-day trip rather than an epic. It is reached by leaving the Watson Lakes trail at the saddle, climbing the ridge above Lower Anderson Lake, and working east through meadows and moraine across the massif — a long undulating traverse rather than a climb, and the part of the day that eats the time. From camp the summit is a short ascent to the southeast, and it is possible to reach the top without crossing glaciers at all, which is what makes this a scramble for a competent party rather than a rope-up. Immediately north the ground falls away past post-glacial moraine to the saddle above the green lake below the glacier, and that is the line onward for anyone continuing east or north across the range. It is a fully exposed shelf with nothing to shelter behind and the weather here comes across from Baker with no warning. The season is roughly mid-July into September; earlier and the traverse is a long snow slope, later and the water is gone.

bivy.permit: This camp sits on the boundary country between the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness and North Cascades National Park, and which one it falls in decides whether you need a permit at all. Ask specifically when you plan the trip: the Forest Service side needs no overnight permit, while the park side needs a backcountry permit written for the correct cross-country zone. No campfires on either side of the line. Camp on snow, rock or gravel and never on the heather, keep well back from water, and pack out all waste — on snow and glacier that means blue bags carried out.
bivy.capacity: Open ground for a couple of small parties on gravel, rock and heather about half a mile northeast of the summit; informal, with nothing built and no toilet

bivy.name: Watson Lakes

road.name: Baker Lake Road (FR-11) to FR-1106/FR-1107, Anderson & Watson Lakes Trailhead
road.driveNote: FR-1107 (Anderson-Watson Road) has been closed at Mile Post 3.8 by a washout since July 8, 2026, with no end date given on the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert still posted on 25 September 2026 — this blocks vehicle access to the standard Anderson & Watson Lakes Trailhead. bivy.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
bivy.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

bivy.name: Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp
bivy.notes: Narrow lateral moraine at the southern edge of the Crooked Thumb Glacier, reached from Perfect Pass across the Challenger Glacier and down through the notch west of Challenger. The base camp for Crooked Thumb and Phantom from the north. Fully exposed to weather.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and glacier melt only
bivy.permit: North Cascades NP backcountry permit (cross-country zone)
bivy.capacity: A few tents on a narrow moraine

bivy.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
bivy.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. With both Whatcom Camp and Graybeal closed there is currently no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
bivy.water: Brush Creek drainage — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
bivy.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

bivy.name: Improvised bivouacs on the Challenger Glacier and the crest south of Challenger
bivy.notes: Spectre Peak sits well down the crest south of Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle is a multi-pitch rock climb off the glacier, so parties working the far end of the chain sometimes take a night out on the ice rather than commit to a very long day from Perfect Pass or Challenger Arm. These are made rather than found — a platform stamped into snow, or a gravel patch on a rib — and quality is entirely a matter of what the party can dig. There is no shelter and no water, crevasse hazard is present wherever you put the tent, and it only makes sense with a settled forecast. Anyone unwilling to melt snow for every drop should sleep at Challenger Arm or Perfect Pass instead and accept the longer day.
bivy.water: None. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs — carry water up or melt snow, and assume there is nothing to find.
bivy.permit: Still inside the Challenger cross-country zone and still needs a wilderness permit with that night assigned to it. On the glacier the surface rule takes care of itself, but human waste MUST be carried out in a blue bag; there is no burying it here. No fires. Party limit 6.
bivy.capacity: One party, often on a levelled snow platform or a single gravel ledge

bivy.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
bivy.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

bivy.name: Luna Cirque high camp (near Lousy Lake)
Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
bivy.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. With both Whatcom Camp and Graybeal closed there is currently no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
bivy.water: Brush Creek drainage — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
bivy.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

bivy.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
bivy.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

bivy.name: Improvised bivouacs on the Challenger Glacier and the crest south of Challenger
bivy.notes: Spectre Peak sits well down the crest south of Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle is a multi-pitch rock climb off the glacier, so parties working the far end of the chain sometimes take a night out on the ice rather than commit to a very long day from Perfect Pass or Challenger Arm. These are made rather than found — a platform stamped into snow, or a gravel patch on a rib — and quality is entirely a matter of what the party can dig. There is no shelter and no water, crevasse hazard is present wherever you put the tent, and it only makes sense with a settled forecast. Anyone unwilling to melt snow for every drop should sleep at Challenger Arm or Perfect Pass instead and accept the longer day.
bivy.water: None. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs — carry water up or melt snow, and assume there is nothing to find.
bivy.permit: Still inside the Challenger cross-country zone and still needs a wilderness permit with that night assigned to it. On the glacier the surface rule takes care of itself, but human waste MUST be carried out in a blue bag; there is no burying it here. No fires. Party limit 6.
bivy.capacity: One party, often on a levelled snow platform or a single gravel ledge

bivy.name: Whatcom Pass
Perfect Pass
Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
bivy.notes: These are the camps that put the eastern peaks in range, and they are the reason parties carry a full glacier kit past Itswoot Ridge. The col between the Dana and Dome glaciers holds a couple of rock rings around 7,470 ft, and further east the Dome-Chickamin col is a genuine high camp with figures around 8,000 ft and above quoted for it. From that eastern col the Chickamin Glacier is the highway to Sinister Peak, whose North Face and Southwest Route are both reached across it, and on to the three Gunsight Range summits beyond, which are granite spires ringed by the Chickamin and Blue glaciers and among the most remote objectives in the state. Parties on the Gunsight peaks routinely cross the Chickamin twice in a day from a camp on this ground. Season is short: the glaciers are best covered from July into August, later brings open crevasses and bare ice, and there is no water, no shelter and no quick way down from any of it.
bivy.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek register. Camp on snow, rock or ice. Pack out human waste, which matters more here than anywhere else in the zone because the meltwater below runs straight into the glacier-fed creeks.
bivy.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.

bivy.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
bivy.notes: This exists because of the brush, and the brush is the single most important thing to understand about the south end. From the Downey Creek trailhead at 1,440 ft the Downey Creek trail runs about six easy forested miles to Sixmile Camp; after that the abandoned Bachelor Creek trail deteriorates badly. The first two miles are tolerable, then it crosses to the south side and turns into slide alder and avalanche deadfall, with reports of sixty or more trees over the trail and long sections where following it is closer to bushwhacking than hiking. Parties routinely take nine to eleven hours from the car to Cub Lake and a slow group with heavy packs can lose the trail entirely. Splitting the approach with a night around the 4,500 ft meadows near the head of the creek is the honest answer for anyone who is not fast, and it is why some parties choose to enter from Cascade Pass and exit here rather than the other way round, so the brush is done downhill and with lighter packs. There is a north-side line through open forest paralleling the creek that some report as better than the trail itself. Everything about this approach is currently harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road is closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under an order running to the start of 2028 unless lifted sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.
bivy.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
bivy.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.

bivy.name: Cub Lake
bivy.notes: Roughly 12 miles and about 3,900 ft of gain from the Downey Creek trailhead, reached by a steep switchbacking descent off the Bachelor Creek meadows and a walk around the north shore. Parties report anywhere from six hours to eleven getting here, which is a fair measure of how much the brush and the pack weight vary. It is the south-end hub: from the lake the trail climbs to Itswoot Ridge for Spire Point and Dome Peak, and everything on the Chickamin side including Sinister Peak and the Gunsight summits starts from the same ground. Because it is the established camp it also takes the impact, and there is a reasonable argument for camping on the ridge above instead where the ground is less worn, at the cost of carrying water. Coming out, this is where the traverse ends and the brush begins.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable all season. This is the last certain water for anyone heading up onto the ridge and glaciers, and the first on the way out.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Downey Creek trailhead. Camp 100 feet back from the shore. Practically speaking no fires, and the site is heavily enough used that the surrounding wood is already gone.
bivy.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.

bivy.name: Itswoot Ridge
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Dome Peak is the other objective, reached over the Dana Glacier and the Dome Glacier above. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.
bivy.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
bivy.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

bivy.name: Wallace Creek basin ridge camp
bivy.notes: This is the established high camp for Lincoln and the one nearly every ascent uses. It sits on the ridge overlooking the Wallace Creek basin, right at the last stand of trees, with the Black Buttes and the summit block in view above. Reaching it means walking the road to about the seventh switchback, picking up the old track that leads toward Rankin Creek, scrambling into the basin, passing east Rankin Lake, then climbing mellow snow north to the saddle near 5,480 ft and east up the basin below Seward to the ridge. From here the X Couloir on the southwest face and the north ridge are both single-push summit days, and both are long, steep, exposed snow and ice, which is why the camp is high. The peak is in condition in spring, when fresh snow has mostly stopped falling but nights are still cold enough to hold the snow, ice and rock together; by high summer the face becomes loose and dangerous. Expect the trees to be buried and the ground to be snow. Nothing here is sheltered from weather coming off Baker.
bivy.water: Running water is unreliable at this height. In spring, when the peak is in condition, you melt snow, which is what nearly every party does. Later in the year expect to carry from the tarns at the saddle below
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, inside the Mount Baker Wilderness, whose boundary you cross on the way up into the basin. No overnight wilderness permit is required and none is issued for this area. Party size is capped at twelve. A Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass covers parking at the road end. This is national forest, not national park, so no park backcountry permit applies and none can be obtained for it. Stoves rather than fires, and pack out everything including waste on snow
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents on the last flat ground beside the highest trees; more parties than that and people are pitching on open snow

bivy.name: Middle Fork Nooksack road switchbacks
bivy.notes: Sleeping at the vehicle the night before is the normal way to start this climb, because the approach is long and parties want to be walking in the dark. The switchbacks above the road's lower section give rough pullouts around 2,650 to 3,420 ft depending on how far the surface lets you drive; past the first switchback the brush closes in and the potholes get serious, and a small car will not make it far. With the road currently barriered at milepost 7 the practical bivouac is wherever the closure puts you, and the Rankin Creek switchbacks are then a long walk or bike ride away — a bicycle to the closure point is worth considering. No elevation is given here because the usable spot depends entirely on how far up the road is open in a given season, which changes.
bivy.water: Creeks cross and run down the road in spring, and Rankin Creek is nearby. Treat anything you take
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, outside the wilderness boundary at this elevation. Dispersed roadside camping, no permit, no reservation. Check the current fire restrictions before lighting anything and expect fires to be banned outright in dry spells; a stove is the safe assumption. Pack out all rubbish
bivy.capacity: Roadside pullouts at the lower switchbacks take a couple of vehicles each; there are no built sites, no tables and no toilets

bivy.name: East Rankin Lake
bivy.notes: The lower of the two natural stopping places on the approach, in the Rankin Creek basin below the saddle. It is the sensible camp for a party that started late, that is walking extra road miles because of the washout, or that wants an easier carry on day one and a longer summit day on day two. From here the route continues north on easy-angled snow to the small saddle and then east into the upper basin, so nothing is wasted. The cost is close to a thousand feet of climbing left over for summit morning on a route where the difficulties start high. In spring the lake is a flat white plain and easy to camp on; later in the season the basin brushes up and the ground around the water is soggy.
bivy.water: The lake, once it has melted out. In the spring climbing season it is frozen and buried, so plan on melting snow
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest and Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required, twelve-person party limit, recreation pass for the vehicle at the road end. No campfires above treeline; use a stove. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and keep off the heather when it is out
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents around the lake basin on snow or, late in the year, on gravel and heather away from the shore

bivy.name: Saddle tarns above Rankin Creek
bivy.notes: The small saddle north of the Rankin basin, with a pair of tarns beside it, sitting between east Rankin Lake and the climb east into the upper basin below Seward. It is a stopgap rather than a destination: only a few hundred feet above the lake and still well short of the ridge camp, so it is chosen mostly by parties caught by weather or darkness on the way up. It is a windy notch, which is worth knowing before you commit to it in a storm. The one thing it does well is mark the point where the approach turns from valley travel to open alpine snow, so it is a useful place to re-assess conditions before carrying a heavy load higher.
bivy.water: Two small tarns sit right at the saddle. They are usually still under snow through the spring climbing season, so treat them as a summer source and otherwise melt snow
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit, twelve-person limit, recreation pass at the road end. Stove only
bivy.capacity: One or two tents on the flats beside the small lakes; informal ground with no established site

approach_variants.name: Middle Fork Nooksack Road (FR-38) and Rankin Creek to the treeline camp, then the southwest basin
approach_variants.notes:
This is the more direct way to the X Couloir: from the SOUTH via the Middle Fork Nooksack River Road (FR-38). The southwest face can also be reached from Heliotrope Ridge through the Thunder Glacier cirque, a less direct line with more glacier travel; do not confuse either with the north-facing Coleman side, which leads to the other route on this mountain.

Drive FR-38 toward its mile-12.5 switchback and start walking the old decommissioned road around Point 4481 toward Rankin Creek. Snow travel — often by bike or snowshoe on the lower stretch — leads past East Rankin Lake near 5,120 ft and up into the basin to a sheltered camp at treeline around 6,100 ft, by the highest trees in the basin below Seward Peak. Roughly seven miles and 3,350 ft of gain to camp.

ACCESS: as of mid-2026 FR-38 is closed at milepost 7 by a washout from the December 2025 floods, with no confirmed repair timeline, and a separate gate at Wallace Creek near mile 10 closes the road 1 December to 15 June for elk calving. Confirm the drivable road-end with the Mount Baker Ranger District before the trip; the length of the approach varies year to year.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Apr-Jun. A spring snow climb; essentially never done in summer, because what makes it climbable is continuous snow rather than the rubble underneath
hazards: A bergschrund crossing that must be done cold and early
1,500 ft of 30-40 degree snow with a steep serac step, all of it above a long runout
FR-38 flood damage with no repair timeline, plus an elk-calving gate closed 1 Dec - 15 Jun
A gully that funnels rockfall and spindrift after storms
A descent that is a real rappel sequence off pickets and slung horns, not a walk-off
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE HIGHEST TREES IN THE BASIN ARE THE CAMP, AND THE CAMP IS THE LAST THING YOU CAN NAVIGATE TO. Above treeline the southwest side of Lincoln is open snow and there is nothing to hold on to in cloud. So the arrival marker is vegetative rather than topographic: climb until the trees stop, and camp at the last of them, below Seward Peak, around 6,100 ft.

THE BERGSCHRUND IS THE BASE OF THE CLIMB. From camp an alpine start takes you into the southwest basin and to the schrund while the snow is still cold and firm. Above it is roughly 1,500 ft of 30-40 degree snow with a steep serac step in it.

DO NOT EXPECT ONE CLEAN COULOIR — THIS IS THE TRAP THE NAME SETS. Parties who have climbed and skied it describe it as less a couloir and more a series of steep chutes and faces, and the line drops from the high point to the highest notch, then down a narrow chute, and trends right out of view. So 'find the obvious couloir' is the wrong instruction and will have you standing in the basin looking for something that is not there. Work from the notch downward: the correct line is the one that connects to the HIGHEST notch on the skyline, and it is narrow where it leaves the basin.

THE SERAC STEP IS THE CONFIRMATION. Somewhere in that 1,500 ft you meet a steep serac step. A line with no ice step in it is not the X Couloir.

AND THE ASPECT SETTLES THE COARSE ERROR: this route faces SOUTHWEST and this approach reaches it from Rankin Creek. If you are standing on the Coleman Glacier looking at a shaded north-facing cirque, you are under the other route on this mountain.

bivy.name: Watson Lakes designated camps
bivy.notes: The substance of this zone and the best camping anywhere near these three peaks. It is a genuinely short walk — about two miles from the road end, through forest to a meadow junction, over a saddle at around 4,700 ft and down to the pair of lakes at 4,400 ft — which makes it the rare alpine camp in the North Cascades that costs a heavy pack almost nothing. Mount Watson rises straight above: from the lakes the line works up the north side, traverses to the large col near 5,900 ft between the East Peak and the jumbled western summits, then takes heather and treed slopes west to the basin under the true summit, a heather and dirt gully on the south side of the summit block, and a short exposed class two to three ridge to the top where many parties want a fixed line. For Bacon Peak this is the staging night rather than the base, since the summit is a long way east across the massif. The lakes are notoriously buggy through midsummer and hold snow into early season. Everything here is heavily used and the designation exists because it was being trampled.
bivy.water: The lakes and a nearby stream, reliable through the season. There is no potable water on the road or the trail, so treat everything.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, inside the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, which the trail enters at the saddle before dropping to the lakes. No overnight permit is required or issued. A recreation pass must be displayed at the trailhead, and between December and April a state Sno-Park permit is required at the Anderson Creek Sno-Park instead. CAMPING IS ALLOWED ONLY IN THE DESIGNATED SITES and campfires are prohibited outright — carry a stove. Standard wilderness rules otherwise: keep the party small, camp on rock or bare ground rather than in the heather, pack out everything, and secure food overnight since there is no hardware provided.
bivy.capacity: Designated sites at the two lakes, first come first served with no reservations, plus a backcountry toilet. Flat ground is mostly rock outcrop along the shoreline; the upper lake takes the larger share of parties.

bivy.name: Camp on slopes below Mount Watson (~5,400 ft)
Anderson Creek road end, Watson Lakes trailhead
bivy.notes: This is the road rather than a campsite, because on this side of the massif the road decides what the trip is. It is a rare thing in this range — a driveable gravel road that delivers you to 4,200 ft, within two miles of an alpine lake basin — and it is why the Anderson and Watson Lakes are the substance of this zone rather than a footnote. THE ROAD IS THE PROBLEM AS OF 2026: an atmospheric river in December 2025 cut a washout in FS 1107 at around mile three to four, well below the road end, and that failure has closed the trailhead and the Sno-Park with no quick fix. When it is in force the whole approach becomes four or five miles of road walking with 1,500 ft of gain before the trail even starts, which turns a comfortable overnight on Mount Watson into a serious two-day trip and puts Bacon Peak out of reach for most parties from this side. Confirm the road with the ranger district before driving out, and if it is open, sleeping in the lot the night before is a normal and sensible way to save the morning. The road holds snow late and is not usually driveable to the end until well into the season.
bivy.water: None at the road end. Carry what you need for the evening; the first water is at the lakes, which are close enough that most parties simply walk in.
bivy.permit: Recreation pass required, and a state Sno-Park permit instead from December through April. This is national forest outside the wilderness boundary, so a night in the lot or a pullout is generally tolerated, but never in a way that narrows the road or blocks a turning place. The wilderness rules start at the saddle above.
bivy.capacity: A modest gravel lot at the road end with room for perhaps a dozen vehicles and a few flat spots to sleep beside them; no facilities, and it fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lower Anderson Lake
bivy.notes: Half a mile down from the second trail junction and a hundred feet above the Watson Lakes, and the more useful of the two basins for anyone climbing rather than hiking, because BACON PEAK'S APPROACH RUNS DIRECTLY ABOVE IT. From the saddle about 1.4 miles up the Watson Lakes trail a boot path climbs south onto the ridge high above this lake and opens into the meadows that lead east across the massif toward the Bacon summits, so a party camped here is on the line rather than beside it. It also solves the problem the designated sites create — when the four-and-four at the Watson Lakes are taken there is nowhere legal to squeeze in, and this basin is the fallback. Anderson Butte, a former lookout site with a long view over Baker Lake and across to Baker and Shuksan, is a short spur off the same trail junction and is worth the twenty minutes on an evening you are not going anywhere. Bugs are as bad here as at the lakes over the saddle.
bivy.water: The lake, treated. Dependable all season.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. This lake sits on the trail before it crosses into the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, so the strict designated-site rule that governs the lakes beyond the saddle does not apply in the same way here — but the campfire ban, the small-party expectation and the pack-it-all-out rule should be treated as applying regardless, because the ground is identical and equally fragile. Recreation pass at the trailhead; Sno-Park permit instead from December through April. No permit is issued for an overnight and none is needed.
bivy.capacity: A small number of informal sites at the lake with a backcountry privy; quieter than the sister lakes over the saddle and usually the one with space left

bivy.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
bivy.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. With both Whatcom Camp and Graybeal closed there is currently no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
bivy.water: Brush Creek drainage — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
bivy.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

bivy.name: Twin Rocks and Stillwell Camps, Little Beaver
bivy.notes: These two sit at the hinge between the Little Beaver and Big Beaver trails and are what make the water-taxi loop practical: get dropped at the Little Beaver landing, walk up to Whatcom Pass for Whatcom Peak and Challenger, and exit over Beaver Pass and down Big Beaver, or run it the other way. For the Northern Pickets they are through-camps on a long walk rather than climbing bases. The Ross Lake water taxi is chartered by the boat rather than per head, takes about six people, needs a reservation, and only runs during the resort's summer season — outside it, plan on walking in from Ross Dam and adding a day at each end.
bivy.water: Little Beaver Creek at both — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camps, reservable or walk-up. Both closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure, which covers Little Beaver from Ross Lake to Whatcom Pass.
bivy.capacity: Twin Rocks: two 6-person sites, party limit 6. Stillwell: four 4-person sites, party limit 4

bivy.name: Luna Cirque floor
bivy.notes: The floor of the great bowl beneath Luna Peak, walled on three sides, and the low point of the traverse that enters by Access Creek and Luna Pass and leaves over Challenger Gap onto Wiley Ridge. It sits directly under the eastern side of the crest that carries Spectre Peak, and parties coming off Challenger sometimes drop southeast into it rather than reversing the glacier. As a bed it is a long way below Luna Col, which remains the right camp for climbing Luna Peak itself; the value of the cirque is that it links the Access Creek and Wiley Ridge sides without going back over the top. Getting in and out is trackless in both directions and the brush low in Access Creek, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
bivy.water: Meltwater running off the cirque walls, and a shallow seasonal lake on the floor that becomes warm sand as the summer dries it out. Early season is wet and late season is a search.
bivy.permit: Luna cross-country zone, walk-up only — it cannot be reserved, and a party that has already driven, boated and walked in can still be turned away if the night's slots are taken. Carry a fallback itinerary. Camp on sand, rock or snow, 100 ft from water, no fires.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on sand, gravel and slab; party limit 6

bivy.name: Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine high camp
Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
bivy.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. CLOSED under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

bivy.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
bivy.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. With both Whatcom Camp and Graybeal closed there is currently no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
bivy.water: Brush Creek drainage — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
bivy.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

bivy.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
bivy.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

bivy.name: Luna Camp

climate.typical: Maritime North Cascades alpine climate: heavy winter/spring snowpack, a relatively short and unpredictable weather window in summer, and frequent Pacific frontal systems that can bring rain or snow at any elevation with little warning.

bySeason.fall: September can still go but rock and gully snow degrade further, increasing rockfall/looseness; shorter daylight extends the already long approach days.
bySeason.spring: Deep, often unstable snowpack and difficult/impassable creek crossings on the approach; road/trail access frequently limited by residual winter damage.
bySeason.summer: July-August offers the most consolidated snow on the glacier approach and the most stable rock in the summit gully; still expect afternoon thunderstorm risk.
bySeason.winter: Essentially inaccessible for climbing given the multi-day approach, avalanche hazard, and (currently) the FR26 road closure.

bivy.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
bivy.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

bivy.name: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
bivy.notes: This is the Hannegan Pass approach rather than a Ross Lake one, and it is how Spectre Peak is actually reached — in past ascents parties bivouacked near the summit of Easy Peak, dropped to the Imperfect Impasse and climbed through to the western slope of the range. From the trailhead you go over Hannegan Pass and down past Boundary and Copper Creek camps, then ford the Chilliwack River just above where Easy Creek comes in, and climb about five miles of ridge to open ground above 6,000 ft, with Easy Peak at 6,615 ft carrying the anchors of an old lookout. The sting is what comes after: reaching Perfect Pass from here means descending roughly 1,000 ft to get around the Imperfect Impasse gap and climbing back up, which is why parties who intend to camp at Perfect Pass often prefer the Whatcom Pass side instead. Two days in before any climbing starts.
bivy.water: Seasonal tarns scattered along the crest. Some hold water and some are dry in the same summer, which makes this the least predictable water on the route. Fill at the Chilliwack River before starting up.
bivy.permit: Park wilderness permit required. This side is served by the wilderness information centres on both the Mount Baker Highway and at Marblemount, and the ranger will decide whether your night goes onto a designated camp or a cross-country zone — ask rather than assume, because the answer changes what the rest of the itinerary can say. Walk-up. Fires prohibited. Approved food storage required, and above treeline there is nothing to hang from, so a canister is the practical answer.
bivy.capacity: Small — one or two parties on the ridge crest; party limit 6

bivy.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass

Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. With both Whatcom Camp and Graybeal closed there is currently no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
bivy.water: Brush Creek drainage — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
bivy.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

bivy.name: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side
bivy.notes: This is the base for Glacier Peak's Kennedy Glacier and for the Frostbite Ridge line above it, and since the White Chuck approach died it is the only practical way at the mountain's north and west sides. The walk in is long even when the road is open — the Suiattle River trail runs about seven miles to the river bridge and the crest trail then carries you south toward Kennedy Ridge, so this is a full day before the climbing camp is even in sight. Kennedy Creek has no bridge and will not get one; the standard tactic is to camp short of it and cross in the morning when the flow is at its lowest, using whatever logs are currently in place rather than wading the main channel. Above the forest the route climbs the ridge and the glacier toward the saddle between the Kennedy and Vista glaciers at around 8,000 feet, where bivouac sites exist for parties willing to sleep on snow and rock with no shelter and no clean water. With the road washed out the trailhead is still reachable on foot or by bike from the closure point, which adds roughly nine miles each way to an approach that was already the longest on the mountain.
bivy.water: Glacier Creek and Kennedy Creek are both right there and both silty with glacial flour — let it settle or filter accordingly. Higher on the ridge water disappears entirely by late season and has to be carried or melted.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Suiattle road end. Stove only above the forest. approach_variants.name: From the north — Cascade Pass and the glacier corridor
approach_variants.notes: Lizard has no trailhead of its own and is normally met partway through the high traverse rather than approached. From the Cascade River Road end, the maintained trail switchbacks up a forested rib and then traverses meadow and talus to Cascade Pass, which is the last built tread of the trip. Leave it there and work south and east across the Mixup flank on boot path, talus and snow to the Cache Glacier and Cache Col, then drop the steep snow on the far side to the tarn at Kool-Aid Lake. Beyond, the Red Ledge cuts the cliff band west of Art's Knoll, then the Middle Cascade Glacier leads to the Spider-Formidable col and down to Yang Yang Lakes. From there the line climbs past Le Conte Mountain, crosses the Le Conte Glacier to the gap north of Sentinel Peak, and crosses the South Cascade Glacier to the col at its head before dropping into the White Rock Lakes basin. Lizard is the side trip from that camp: climb back out of the basin northeast to the broad notch on the peak's south ridge.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, once the Cache Col snow has consolidated and the Red Ledge is clear of verglas; the whole corridor has to be in condition, not just the peak.

approach_variants.baseFinding: THE COL IS THE REFERENCE, AND IT IS THE ONLY PLACE ON THIS MOUNTAIN WHERE YOU CAN SEE BOTH BASINS AT ONCE. The notch you want is the broad pass in the south ridge at a little over 6,800 ft, roughly two thousand feet of horizontal distance west of the summit. Standing in it, White Rock Lakes should be below you to the southwest and South Cascade Glacier ice below you to the northeast; the ground rising off the col toward the high point is a single broad, blocky, loose ridge of only about six hundred vertical feet, and the top of it is visible from where you stand. If you cannot see both the lakes and the glacier from the notch, or if what rises above you is far more than six hundred feet, or if you have to step back onto glacier ice to keep going up, you are at the wrong gap in the ridge. Nothing on the correct line is harder than hands-on scrambling on loose blocks — if you meet a step that makes you want a rope, you have drifted off the crest onto the flanks, where the rubble is worst. Stay near the crest and keep the party out of each other's fall line rather than strung out directly below.

approach_variants.name: From the south — Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek (closed at present)
approach_variants.notes: Not usable at present: the Suiattle River Road is closed at milepost 4 until at least January 2028, and washouts cut off the Downey Creek Trailhead. Before the closure this was the other end of the same corridor. From the Downey Creek Trailhead on the Suiattle River Road, Downey Creek Trail #768 enters wilderness within the first half mile and climbs gently through old growth, crossing tributary creeks that run high in early season, to the Bachelor Creek junction. The Bachelor Creek path is unmaintained, steadily steeper, and notorious for blowdown, with an alder and slide-alder band around 3,800 to 4,400 ft that becomes a genuine bushwhack when snow has not flattened it. It fords Bachelor Creek itself, which runs fast and cold with snowmelt. Above treeline the tread breaks into meadows near Bachelor Meadows and reaches Cub Lake, reliable water and a common first camp. A steep, often snow-covered pitch gains Itswoot Ridge; from there the route climbs to Spire Col, descends the Dana Glacier to White Rock Lakes, and regains the col on Lizard's south ridge from the lakes.

approach_variants.baseFinding: THE COL IS THE REFERENCE, AND IT IS THE ONLY PLACE ON THIS MOUNTAIN WHERE YOU CAN SEE BOTH BASINS AT ONCE. Climbing out of the White Rock Lakes basin you reach a broad pass in the south ridge at a little over 6,800 ft, roughly two thousand feet of horizontal distance west of the summit. From it, White Rock Lakes lie below to the southwest and South Cascade Glacier ice lies below to the northeast; the ground rising toward the high point is one broad, blocky, loose ridge of only about six hundred vertical feet, with its top visible from where you stand. If you cannot see both the lakes and the glacier from the notch, or if what rises above you is far more than six hundred feet, or if you have to step back onto glacier ice to keep gaining height, you are at the wrong gap. Nothing on the correct line is harder than hands-on scrambling — a step that makes you want a rope means you have drifted off the crest onto the flanks, which carry the worst of the rubble. Stay near the crest, and keep the party abreast rather than strung out directly below one another.

days.note: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead, climb switchbacks to Cascade Pass (5,400 ft, 3.7 mi) then continue up the Sahale Arm Trail to the permitted Sahale Glacier Camp at 7,600 ft. Most parties treat this as a half-day carry so they're fresh for an early alpine start the next morning.
days.title: Approach to Sahale Glacier Camp
days.objective: Reach Sahale Glacier Camp (7,600 ft) as base for the Horseshoe/Buckner traverse

days.note: Alpine start down off Sahale Arm into Horseshoe Basin, crossing snow/talus past old Davenport Mine relics to the base of Horseshoe's summit block. A short, exposed 5.2 step (rope, light rack, 30-60m) gains the true summit; most parties downclimb or make one short rappel back to the ledge. After returning to camp, break it down and hike the full ~5.7 mi / 4,000 ft back down to the trailhead the same day, making for a long but standard second day.
days.title: Summit push and full exit

schedule.label: Leave Sahale Glacier Camp
schedule.detail: Alpine start to be off the summit block before afternoon weather builds.

schedule.label: Drop into Horseshoe Basin
schedule.detail: Cross snowfield/talus below the Sahale-Buckner col, using old mining remains as landmarks.

schedule.label: Reach base of Horseshoe's summit block
schedule.detail: Scramble Class 3-4 terrain up the snowfield to the final rock step.

schedule.label: Rope up for the 5.2 crux
schedule.detail: Short technical pitch to the true summit; many parties solo-belay or simul with a light rack.

schedule.label: Summit, then downclimb/rappel

schedule.label: Back at Sahale Glacier Camp

itinerary.totalNote: A 2-day trip is the norm: ~5.7 mi/4,000 ft up to Sahale Glacier Camp on Day 1, then a long ~9-10 hr, ~9 mi summit-and-exit Day 2 with a short roped 5.2 step near the top; very fit parties do climb it car-to-car in a single ~12-16 hr day instead.

itinerary.cal: Access is via Ross Lake Resort's water taxi (SR-20 to Ross Dam, then boat up-lake to the Hozomeen campground at the head of the lake) since the historic Silver-Skagit Road border crossing from Hope, BC has been closed to both vehicle and foot traffic since the COVID-19 pandemic and remains closed as of 2026; best attempted mid-July through September once the west basin snow/water sources are known.

days.note: An easy 1.5-mile forest walk from the Hozomeen Lake trailhead gives way to a rougher off-trail push: crossing Hozomeen Creek, fighting devil's club and windfall, then climbing red scree and heather into the west basin below a broad slab wall. Most parties reach the 6,800 ft saddle camp by mid-afternoon, drop the overnight gear, and — if weather and energy allow — continue straight up for the summit the same day, returning to camp before dark. The final headwall below the summit is a short, exposed 5.6 step; bring a rope and rack a few pieces plus a sling for the fixed rap anchors used by past parties.

days.note: A relaxed morning — several parties report waiting for wind to die down before packing up — followed by a few hours of descending the west basin and forest trail back to the car. No fixed schedule needed; it's a straightforward reversal of Day 1's approach.

best_season: July through September is the reliable window: rock is dry and at its grippiest, though north-aspect gullies and the approach can hold lingering snow into early July in heavy-snowpack years, and late-summer afternoons can bring thunderstorms or wildfire smoke. Road/trail access currently overrides season as the limiting factor — as of mid-2026 the FSR 38 approach is closed by flood damage with no repair date, so check Mount Baker Ranger District alerts regardless of time of year.

approach_variants.name: Skyline Divide Trail #678 and the long open ridge south to Chowder Ridge
approach_variants.notes:
ACCESS FIRST: from Glacier, WA drive SR-542 about a mile past the Glacier Public Service Center to Glacier Creek Road (FS-39), turn right, then immediately left onto Deadhorse Road (FS-37). FS-37 normally runs 12.7 miles to the Skyline Divide trailhead. FS-37 is currently closed to vehicles at mile 0.03 while the 2021 flood washout at milepost 3.1 is repaired, so the trailhead is not reachable by vehicle. Confirm before planning around it.

When open, Skyline Divide Trail #678 climbs through old-growth switchbacks into meadows and reaches the ridge crest at about 2 miles and its high point near 6,563 ft at about 4.5 miles. From there the route is cross-country along the open ridge — roughly three miles of it — to Chowder Ridge and the base of Hadley's summit block.

The trail's high point on the crest near 6,563 ft is the landmark parties use to re-find the maintained trail on the way back.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Aug-Oct — this trailhead may not currently be reachable at all
hazards: FS-37 closed at mile 0.03 during washout repair — the trailhead is not drivable until the work ends
Three miles of cross-country open ridge with no tread and no cairns
A short Class 3 step above loose scree and talus
Two unmarked divides converging on one summit, with very different roads at the bottom
No water once past the meadows
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE 6,600 FT VIEWPOINT IS THE GATE, IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. It is where maintained trail ends and where you rejoin it. In cloud it is the only reliable waypoint on this approach, because everything beyond it is three miles of undifferentiated open ridge. Note it on the way out — parties who do not, spend the return walking a crest that all looks the same.

THE CREST IS THE HANDRAIL. From the viewpoint the route runs SOUTH along the ridge and then SOUTHEAST along Chowder Ridge, roughly three miles in all. Keep the crest under your feet with air on both sides; this ridge has heather benches falling away either side and it is easy to drift onto one and lose the line.

ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING: the summit block is a SHORT CLASS 3 STEP above loose scree and talus — the last stretch of the day and the only scrambling on it. Walking stops, one short step of rock, summit. That is the whole climb, and it is the test: if you are scrambling for a long time, you are on a false feature; if you have not left your feet, you are not there.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE OTHER APPROACH TO THIS SAME BLOCK: Cougar Divide arrives on Chowder Ridge from the NORTH-WEST after crossing near Dobbs Creek, and its trail high point is 5,920 ft. Skyline arrives from the WEST after roughly three miles of ridge from a 6,600 ft viewpoint. If you are descending in poor visibility, going down the wrong divide puts you 11 miles of gravel road away from your car on a road that may itself be washed out.
